fullTitle: Mining Map Software for Exploration Teams | Exploration Maps
h1: Mining Map Software for Exploration Teams
label: Mining Map Software
metaDescription: Browser-based mining and mineral exploration map software. Build claim maps, drill collar plans, target and infrastructure maps from your own GIS files or public registry data, and export figures for decks, reports and news releases.
intro: Exploration Maps is browser-based mining map software for building clean, investor-ready project maps from claim boundaries, drillholes, targets, and your own GIS files — without learning a full desktop GIS system.

sections.h2: What mining map software is used for
sections.body: Mining map software turns raw exploration data — claim boundaries, drill collars, sample points, target outlines, roads — into a single readable map. Geologists, junior mining companies, consultants, and investor relations teams use these maps to show where a project is, what ground a company controls, and what the exploration results look like. The goal is a map that a non-technical reader can understand at a glance, formatted for a slide, a report figure, a website, or a news release.

sections.h2: Why exploration teams need clean project maps
sections.body: A project map is often the first thing an investor, partner, or regulator looks at. A cluttered screenshot from a desktop GIS or a generic satellite image with hand-drawn boxes undermines credibility. Clean maps with a clear legend, scale bar, north arrow, and title block communicate that the work behind them is organized. For capital markets and corporate development teams, map quality is part of how a project is judged.

sections.h2: Claim maps, drillhole maps, target maps, and project overview maps
sections.html: Most exploration programs need a few recurring map types, and Exploration Maps handles each one. A claims map shows the land position and tenure outline. A drill results map shows collars, intercepts, and assay highlights. A target map shows priority areas and anomalies over the claim block. A project overview, or location map, places the property in its regional and infrastructure context. You can build all of these from the same imported data and reuse a consistent style across them.

sections.h2: From data to investor decks, websites, reports, and news releases
sections.body: Once a map is styled, you export it for the channel you need: a 16:9 PNG for an investor deck or PowerPoint slide, a high-resolution image for a company website, a print-ready PDF figure for a technical report, or a clear graphic for a drill-result news release. Because the underlying project is saved, you can update the data and re-export the same map layout when results change, keeping every channel consistent.

sections.h2: Built for non-GIS users
sections.body: Traditional GIS tools are powerful but assume you know about coordinate reference systems, symbology rules, layout composers, and projection handling. Exploration Maps assigns sensible styling automatically when you tag a layer as claims, drillholes, or targets, fits the view to your data, and gives you a layout with the standard map elements already in place. Most users produce a presentable map in their first session without prior GIS training.

sections.h2: Import the data you already have
sections.html: If you already work with GIS files, you can bring them straight in — see turning a Shapefile into a map. Exploration Maps reads Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, and CSV, so most exploration datasets import without conversion. You can also search public mineral claim data directly when you do not have a file to start from.

sections.h2: What belongs on a mineral exploration project map
sections.body: Most exploration project maps are assembled from the same handful of layers. Which ones you show depends on the argument the map is making:

rows: Is the project on ground the company controls?
Where in the world is this?
How hard is it to get to and to service?
Why here, and what is being tested?
What has been drilled, and what came back?

sections.html: A map that shows all six at once usually communicates less than one that shows three. See how to make a professional exploration map for the layout elements that go around them.

faqs.q: Do I need GIS experience to use mining map software?
faqs.a: No. Exploration Maps applies standard styling automatically when you assign a layer role (claims, drillholes, targets) and provides a layout with a legend, scale bar, north arrow, and title block already in place. It is designed for geologists, IR teams, and other non-GIS users.

faqs.q: What file types can I import?
faqs.a: You can import Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, and CSV. CSV files with coordinate columns are mapped using a column mapper so latitude and longitude are assigned correctly.

faqs.q: What can I export?
faqs.a: You can export PNG images for presentations and websites and print-ready PDFs for technical reports. Common ratios such as 16:9 landscape and letter portrait are available for decks and report figures.

fullTitle: BC Mineral Claims Map & Claim Search | Exploration Maps
label: BC Mineral Claims
metaDescription: Search British Columbia mineral claims by tenure number or registered owner, map the boundaries, and track good-to-dates. Public MTO tenure data — verify in Mineral Titles Online.
intro: Exploration Maps helps you turn public British Columbia mineral claim data into a clean project map — search claims, style the blocks, add project details, and export for decks, websites, and reports.

sections.h2: Searching BC mineral claims
sections.body: You can pull public British Columbia mineral claim data into Exploration Maps and use it as the starting point for a project map, rather than rebuilding boundaries by hand. This is useful when you want to review a land position quickly or assemble a map without first exporting and converting files from a government portal.

sections.h2: Turning claim data into a clean project map
sections.body: Raw claim polygons are rarely presentation-ready. Once the claims are loaded, tag the layer as claims for standard styling, add context such as roads and water, choose a basemap, and frame the view. The result is a map a reader can interpret, not a screenshot of a data viewer.

sections.h2: Using claim maps for investor decks and internal review
sections.body: A BC claims map is a core asset for corporate presentations, project web pages, and internal reviews ahead of staking decisions or financings. Because the project is saved, you can update it as the land position changes and re-export the same layout.

sections.h2: Adding labels, project details, roads, targets, and logos
sections.body: Add claim labels, a title block with the project name and date, access roads, target outlines, and your company logo. These details turn a boundary outline into a complete project map that stands on its own in a deck or report.

sections.h2: Exporting clean map graphics
sections.body: Export a PNG for slides and websites or a PDF for print-ready report figures. Maps include a legend, scale bar, north arrow, and title block, so they read as finished figures rather than rough working images.

sections.h2: Researching other companies' ground
sections.html: If you are reviewing competitor land positions or doing deal due diligence, you can also search mineral claims by company name and map the results the same way.

disclaimer: Exploration Maps is not the official British Columbia mineral titles registry. Always verify current claim status, ownership, boundaries, and tenure details through BC Mineral Titles Online (MTO) before relying on a map for staking, transactions, or filings.

faqs.q: Is Exploration Maps the official BC claims registry?
faqs.a: No. Exploration Maps is a mapping tool, not a government registry. The official source for British Columbia mineral claim status, ownership, and tenure is BC Mineral Titles Online (MTO), and you should verify details there before relying on them.

faqs.q: Can I export a BC claims map for an investor deck?
faqs.a: Yes. You can export PNG images sized for presentation slides and websites, or PDF figures for technical reports, with a legend, scale bar, north arrow, and title block included.

faqs.q: Can I add roads, targets, and my logo to a BC claims map?
faqs.a: Yes. You can add access roads, target outlines, claim labels, a project title block, and your company logo to build a complete project map from the claim boundaries.

faqs.q: Can I search mineral claims by company name?
faqs.a: Where the underlying public claim data supports it, yes — you can search by company or holder name to review a company's land position and then map the results. Coverage depends on what the relevant public registry exposes.

faqs.q: Is a claim search map an official ownership record?
faqs.a: No. Maps built from a claim search are for research and visualization only. Always verify current ownership, status, and tenure details through the official government mineral titles registry before relying on them.

faqs.q: What can I use a company-name claim map for?
faqs.a: Common uses include reviewing land positions, competitor research, deal review, and project due diligence, with the output dropped into investor decks, reports, websites, or internal memos.

faqs.q: Which provinces support searching mineral claims by company name?
faqs.a: British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland & Labrador and Yukon. Manitoba is searchable by claim number only, because its public mineral disposition layer does not publish a holder name for a company search to match against.

sections.h2: Why a projected Shapefile may fail
sections.body: A .shp with metre-based coordinates needs its matching .prj so the importer can identify and convert the source projection. Include that file in the archive. If the source projection is unknown, ask the data supplier; changing a filename or guessing a UTM zone will not fix the coordinates.

faqs.q: Do I need to convert my Shapefile first?

faqs.q: Can I try it without my own data?
faqs.a: Yes. Download the fictional Cedar Ridge boundary above, upload it, and compare your map with the finished Claims example.

faqs.q: What should I do when the data appears in the wrong place?
faqs.a: Check the coordinate system, the .prj file for a Shapefile, and longitude/latitude order. Use WGS84 decimal degrees for CSV and GeoJSON.

label: Tenure Monitor
h1: Mineral Tenure Monitoring & Claim Expiry Reminders
metaDescription: Track mineral claim expiry dates and get email reminders before each good-to-date. Monitor 10 British Columbia claims free, including ground you do not own. Verify deadlines in Mineral Titles Online.
intro: Tenure Monitor watches a saved group of British Columbia mineral claims, reads their published good-to-dates, and emails you before each deadline. It also tells you when the government record for a monitored claim changes — a date that moved, an owner added or removed, a title that stopped appearing in the published dataset.

sections.h2: What it does
checklist: Saved groups of claims — a project, a region, a joint venture, or everything you hold
Email reminders at 90, 30 and 1 day before each good-to-date
Change detection on the published government record
A maintenance decision and note against each claim, with an audit trail
Claim table, portfolio map and CSV export
One click from any claim into the map editor

sections.h2: Watch ground you do not own
sections.body: A monitored group is a watch list, not an ownership record. A competitor's claims, a property under evaluation, or the block next to yours can all be monitored with the same reminders as your own ground. Nothing about it is visible to the title holder.

sections.h2: What it deliberately does not do
items: It does not log into Mineral Titles Online, and never stores MTO credentials
It does not file assessment work or pay cash in lieu
It does not register, transfer or acquire title
It does not automatically stake released ground
A reminder from Exploration Maps is not a legal notice from the province
sections.body: It reads public data, calculates dates, sends reminders, records what you decided, and links you to MTO. The transaction stays yours.

sections.h2: Plans
sections.html: The final one-day reminder is on every plan, free included — going quiet the day before a deadline is the failure this exists to prevent. Read the good-to-date guide for how the dates work and what moves them.

sections.h2: Coverage
sections.body: Tenure Monitor covers British Columbia. BC publishes a good-to-date as a structured field on every title, which is what makes a reliable countdown possible; other jurisdictions express maintenance obligations differently, and a reminder built on an inferred date would sometimes be wrong about a deadline.
sections.html: Claim search and mapping cover seven Canadian jurisdictions — see the Canadian registry guide.

disclaimer: Government title records and Exploration Maps monitoring results should be verified in the official Mineral Titles Online registry before a transaction or deadline decision.

faqs.q: How do I track mineral claim expiry dates?
faqs.a: Save the claims you care about to a monitored group. Tenure Monitor reads each claim's published good-to-date, counts the days in Pacific time, and emails you at 90, 30 and 1 day beforehand. If the province moves a date, the reminders are recalculated and the outdated ones cancelled.

faqs.q: How many claims can I monitor free?
faqs.a: Ten, in one group, with reminders to one address at 90, 30 and 1 day before each good-to-date. Pro is $29/month and raises that to 50 claims across several groups, with a 7-day reminder and a second recipient.

faqs.q: Does Exploration Maps file my assessment work?
faqs.a: No. Tenure Monitor is read-only with respect to government transactions. It does not log into MTO, store MTO credentials, file work, pay cash in lieu or register title. You do those in Mineral Titles Online yourself; this tells you when they are due.

faqs.q: Can I monitor claims in provinces other than British Columbia?
faqs.a: Not yet. Claim search and mapping cover seven Canadian jurisdictions, but monitoring is BC-only because BC publishes a structured good-to-date on every title. Building a countdown on a date we had to infer would mean sometimes being wrong about a deadline.

faqs.q: Is a reminder a legal notice?
faqs.a: No. It is generated by Exploration Maps from public BC tenure data. It is not a notice from the province and it does not maintain, renew or register any title. Government records control, and important deadlines should be confirmed in MTO.

sections.h2: Search results, company snapshots and saved maps have different dates

rows: The app requests the published service; its publication timing may lag the official registry. Availability and completeness depend on the source.

sections.body: Read the source and date shown with the result or layer. A retrieval date says when data was obtained, not when the government last changed a title. If a date is absent, treat freshness as unverified.

sections.h2: How company matching works
sections.body: Searches compare your query with available published name fields. Exact, possible and weaker candidates help you find spelling variants, but do not prove beneficial ownership, option terms or control. Select titles after checking their identifiers and location. For US results identified as claim-name matches, a familiar company word in a claim name is not an ownership record.

sections.h2: Empty, partial or unavailable results
sections.body: An empty response can mean no matching spelling, the wrong jurisdiction, an unsupported claim type or missing source records. A source outage is a different condition. Read any truncation or scope notice before treating a result as complete. Try a known identifier or consult the official registry; do not infer that ground is available from a missing polygon.

sections.h2: How we check guides and correct errors
sections.body: Exploration Maps prepares these product guides. We compare changed instructions with the current app and use reproducible samples or dated public-data searches for worked examples. Automated checks cover generated pages, links and core editor flows. These checks do not amount to a survey, a title opinion or an independent technical review.
